questions.explanation: Synthesis is the comparison itself, and each correct option performs one: it names an agreement that comes with a discrepancy, or it explains that two studies measured different things and therefore cannot be merged. The other three only carry material across. The tempting reading credits alphabetised lists, opening attributions, and long quotations, but none of them relates anything; a review can be scrupulous in all three and still leave a reader unable to see how the findings fit together.
questions.hint: Ask which moves put two findings into relation with each other.
questions.learningObjective: identify the moves that synthesize findings across sources

options.text: Noting that two studies agree on direction but differ in size

options.misconception: mistakes a list of sources for a comparison between them
options.text: Listing every article read in alphabetical order under the review

options.misconception: treats attribution at the start of a paragraph as integration
options.text: Opening each paragraph with the surname of its main author
Explaining why a later study measured a different group

options.misconception: mistakes the length of a quotation for relational work
options.text: Quoting the longest passage available from the most recent study

answer.exemplar: A strong response says a complete entry shows the source can be found, not that it says what the essay claims, e.g. that the student must still open each source and find the passage behind the sentence.

questions.explanation: A citation records where a source lives, not what it says once found, so complete entries can still point a reader to a passage that never made the claim, and the error stays invisible until somebody opens the book. The tempting reading treats a tidy reference list as evidence of careful reading, but accuracy has two halves: the address must be right, and the content behind the claim must actually be there. Only reading the passage tests the second half.
questions.hint: Ask what a complete entry proves, and what it leaves untested.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a well-formed citation does not establish that a source supports a claim

questions.explanation: Corroboration requires evidence independent of the first report, because a second account copied from the same shop or a newspaper that repeats it adds no new observation at all. Only the separate record supplies something the first report could not. The tempting reading counts how many places repeat the number, but repetition measures circulation rather than confirmation, and a ranking of other shops describes a comparison instead of a measurement of shoplifting.
questions.hint: Ask what would have to be independent of the first report.
questions.learningObjective: state what corroboration of a report requires

options.misconception: counts repetition inside one source as independent evidence
options.text: A second report from the same shop showing similar numbers

options.misconception: treats a repetition of the claim as confirmation of it
options.text: A newspaper article that agrees with the shop's own account

options.misconception: mistakes a ranking of others for independent evidence
options.text: Another researcher ranking the shop first among local shops
An independent record of shoplifting kept by a different group

questions.explanation: A list of figures and tables is an index, so it gives a number, a label, and a page for each display and lets a reader go straight to the one they need instead of scanning the whole report. It holds none of the data itself. The tempting reading treats the list as a summary of results or as a substitute for them, but three-line pointers say nothing about what the measurements were; the numbers a claim needs sit inside the displays, not in the index that names them.
questions.hint: Ask whether the list contains measurements or only addresses.
questions.learningObjective: identify the function of a list of figures and tables

options.text: To let a reader find a particular display without hunting for it

options.misconception: confuses an index of displays with the data it indexes
options.text: To present the underlying data in a compact and readable form

options.misconception: reads a list of displays as cumulative support for a claim
options.text: To prove the report's main claim by gathering every figure at once

options.misconception: assumes a list can substitute for the evidence it indexes
options.text: To replace the displays themselves in a report printed on paper

questions.explanation: A passive construction keeps the grammatical agent off the sentence, and in a methods section that agent is exactly what a reader needs: who stood at the entrance, and who supplied the free sample that may have shaped who stopped. Here the sentence names neither party. The tempting reading finds the form neutral or hunts for some other missing detail, but in a study of what students chose, the party that approached them and offered the incentive is not a stylistic detail at all.
questions.hint: Ask who performed each action, and what their role would let them affect.
questions.learningObjective: analyse what a methods section withholds through passive framing

options.misconception: treats the passive construction as a neutral stylistic choice

options.text: How many students declined to answer the questions they were asked

options.misconception: reads a missing agent as a missing pilot test of the questions
options.text: Whether the questions had been tried out with students beforehand

questions.explanation: Attribution has to follow the chain of speakers, so the interviewee is the source of the report's sentence and the auditor is the source of the underlying claim about the roof, which is why a careful report credits both. The other three break that chain by promoting the writer, by dropping the qualifier, or by claiming the auditor spoke to the researcher. The tempting reading wants one name per sentence, but a second-hand remark credited to a single voice either invents a speaker or hides where the claim began.
questions.hint: Ask who spoke each part, and where the chain of voices begins.
questions.learningObjective: attribute a reported remark to each voice in its chain

options.misconception: credits the interview as though the researcher heard the auditor
options.text: The auditor made the statement, as the report's own research found

options.misconception: flattens a reported remark into the speaker's own claim
options.text: The interviewee said the roof was condemned, without qualification
The interviewee reported what the auditor had told her
The auditor is the original source of the condemnation claim

options.misconception: attributes an opinion to whoever writes the sentence down
options.text: The report's writer is the source of the auditor's judgement
